A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ResFormer/SVFormer research. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring.

before.justification: v3 reports original SlimPajama training experiments, zero-shot benchmark results, architectural ablations, and attention and representation analyses.

after.justification: v4 retains original training and downstream results and adds experiments on learned residual weights, sparse connections, optimization controls, and model representations.

M1.justification: The original fixed averaging method becomes Identity-ResFormer. v4 introduces trainable per-layer mixing coefficients and Sparse-ResFormer, and extends the existing all-history residual option into a learnable Dense-ResFormer (Section 3.3). These change training and connectivity, rather than merely terminology. SVFormer's principal value-sharing rule remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same seven-domain SlimPajama coverage and six zero-shot reasoning benchmarks. The long-sequence scenarios and pretrained Llama/Mistral attention analyses remain represented. Moving downstream evaluation to v4 Appendix A.2 does not change task coverage.

E2.justification: v4 adds learned hidden-state-residual comparators in Table 3 and a post-softmax attention-residual comparator in Table 5. The ResFormer-plus-NeuTRENO comparison from v3 Figure 7 disappears. The principal external comparators—DenseFormer, NeuTRENO, GQA, and CLA—remain, making the comparator changes limited.

E3.justification: v4 changes the primary comparison from smoothed relative training loss to average validation loss; whole-split validation already appeared in v3 Appendix A.6. New experiments introduce learning-rate controls, altered hidden-residual starting points, progressive module removal, and a PCA criterion retaining 99% variance. The core training budget and configuration tables remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 substantially expands analysis of optimization confounds, residual source and destination, coefficient initialization, hidden-versus-value residuals, learned connectivity, module importance, and sparsity/rescaling effects (Sections 4.4–4.6 and Appendix A.1). Conversely, v3's cross-layer approximation-similarity study, value-eigenvalue analysis, and SVFormer sharing/anchor ablations are removed. Most 468M attention visualizations are retained in the appendix.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed counts, confidence intervals, uncertainty bars, or formal significance tests. v4's references to multiple experiments concern configuration searches, not newly documented repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v4 adds extensive validation and diagnostic results, including losses of 2.705 for Learnable-ResFormer and 2.687 for one Sparse-ResFormer configuration (Table 2). Headline parameter/data reductions change from 10.4%/13.6% to 13.3%/15.4% in a scaling comparison now including the learnable variant. The original fixed 82M loss, 2.7117, is retained as rounded 2.712. Per-domain losses from v3 Table 5 disappear, while every downstream score is unchanged between v3 Table 1 and v4 Table 11.

T1.justification: The short block-matrix derivation connecting duplicated-key attention to averaged values and its all-layer extension (v3 Equations 3–5) is omitted. v4 defines its weighted residual family directly instead. No theorem or proof framework is introduced, and the existing entropy definition is retained in Appendix A.1.

C1.justification: v3 centers its contribution on attention concentration and an efficient cross-layer-attention approximation. v4's abstract, introduction, and conclusion instead assert that ordinary hidden residuals inadequately preserve initial token information and position value residuals as a complementary solution. The efficiency claims also increase, while the principal SVFormer cache-reduction claim remains.

C2.justification: v4 develops substantive explanations involving dilution through hidden residuals, why V1 helps differently from V2, learned residual adjustments, and increased attention-module contribution. It interprets optimization controls as evidence beyond accelerated training. New limitations acknowledge imperfect coefficient optimization and absent larger-scale validation; Appendix A.1 discusses potential sparsity costs. The earlier attention-drain mechanism is largely retained there.

D1.justification: v4 documents coefficient initializations and fixed-versus-trainable status for its variants (Section 3.3 and Table 2). It removes v3's code URL, reproducibility statement, and training-curve smoothing instructions. Hardware, optimizer, and core training tables remain. The missing code disclosure does not establish that the repository itself became unavailable.

R1.justification: v4 substantially narrows the KV-efficiency survey, removing discussions and citations covering Mamba/RWKV, quantization, pruning, MLKV, and MLA, among others. It adds Clark et al. (2019), Sun et al. (2024b), and Tyukin et al. (2024) to support information-propagation and module-importance arguments. Positioning relative to hidden-state shortcuts becomes central.

P1.justification: The introduction and method are extensively rewritten, and the experimental narrative is reorganized around scaling, optimization controls, residual design, and post-analysis. Attention diagnostics and downstream evaluation move into the appendix. The title is shortened and the author list changes.

P2.justification: v4 adopts a two-column layout and replaces numerous training-loss plots with validation-loss tables. It adds gradient, learned-weight, similarity, and module-removal displays, including tables showing coefficient initialization. Existing attention panels are regrouped and relocated, and the unchanged downstream table moves to the appendix.

improvement.justification: v4 provides stronger controlled evidence that value residuals help beyond faster optimization or simply adding hidden-state shortcuts (Sections 4.4–4.6), and states concrete optimization and scaling limitations. These strengthen the mechanism argument. The gain is tempered by removal of code-access information, per-domain validation results, and several SVFormer ablations, yielding a limited net improvement in quality.
